items.t: SpaceX Ups Challenge to US Mobile Carriers With Qualcomm Deal
items.d: SpaceX has signed a deal to get hardware from Qualcomm for its planned U.S. terrestrial wireless network. ‘You Can See Everything’ is getting an outer space release and it hasn’t even come out in Europe yet
items.d: It is easier to watch the Elizabeth Holmes documentary "You Can See Everything" in low Earth orbit than in London.
items.fullText: In Brief Posted: 10:10 AM PST · November 4, 2026 Image Credits: Courtesy of A24 Amanda Silberling ‘You Can See Everything’ is getting an outer space release and it hasn’t even come out in Europe yet The film company behind the Elizabeth Holmes documentary “ You Can See Everything ,” A24, posted on Instagram that it granted a request from NASA to screen the film on the International Space Station (ISS). Unless A24 is deceiving us ( why would they? ), it appears that some astronauts can’t wait to come back to Earth to see the film that everyone’s talking about, which has reached number one at the box office. View this post on Instagram “You Can See Everything,” directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, initially debuted in North America with a limited theatrical rollout. The film has been so successful, though, that it’s generating demand from international audiences. Sony Pictures acquired the right to release the film in theaters in Germany, Latin America, South Korea, and other territories, though it hasn’t announced its plans yet. The film won’t come out in the U.K. until November 20, while French viewers will have to wait until December 30. So yes, it is currently easier to watch “You Can See Everything” in low Earth orbit than in London. These hard-working astronauts can take a break from their complex scientific research to address an equally bewildering question: Does Elizabeth Holmes really believe her own lies? Stocks surge as ‘blue tsunami’ puts political uncertainty to rest
items.d: Stocks had their best day in months. Shares of Elon Musk’s SpaceX and Tesla declined, however, after the billionaire spent heavily to support Republicans.
items.fullText: Markets Stocks surge as ‘blue tsunami’ puts political uncertainty to rest Shares of Elon Musk’s SpaceX and Tesla declined, however, after the billionaire spent heavily to support Republican candidates. Listen to this article with a free profile 00:00 00:00 What midterm election results could mean for consumer prices 02:59 Get more news Live on Share Add NBC News to Google Nov. 4, 2026, 1:11 AM EST / Updated Nov. 4, 2026, 4:23 PM EST By Steve Kopack Stocks surged on Wednesday after Democrats won commanding victories in key races across the country, making it immediately clear to investors which party would control the House and Senate. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite closed higher by 1.4%. The broader S&P 500 surged 1.58%, its best day since August. The Russell 2000, which tracks small and medium sized companies, soared 1.5%. The Dow rocketed higher by 1,569 points, its best day since April 2025. A few stocks missed out on the rally, though, most glaringly those of SpaceX and Tesla, which are run by Elon Musk, who spent hundreds of millions of dollars backing Republicans in the midterms. Wall Street welcomed the clarity of the election results, which marked a departure from previous years in which it took several days for decisive projections. “The combination of a large Democratic majority in Congress and President Trump’s statement that he is willing to work with the opposition should act as a break on extreme policy outcomes and bring down risk premia,” said Deutsche Bank’s George Saravelos in a note Wednesday morning. “The market is increasingly likely to interpret surprising policy shifts from the Executive as time-bound by the next Presidential election or the new domestic political configuration,” he added. Since 1946, stocks have been higher a year after every midterm election, noted Truist chief investment officer Keith Lerner. “Simply moving past the uncertainty of the midterms has also often led to a relief rally,” he said. Orbital Matter 3D-printed the first rigid beam in the vacuum of space
items.d: An in-space construction first could be an enabler for the space data centers of the future.
items.fullText: A satellite built by the German startup Orbital Matter 3D-printed a half-meter long beam out of a custom plastic material, in what executives called a first for a free-flying spacecraft in orbit, and a step toward constructing large structures in space. The company’s small satellite, Replicator 2, was launched on a SpaceX rideshare mission this summer, with four of the company’s 3D printers onboard. Each printer can create a rigid, cylindrical beam by extruding coils of resin that are cured by an ultraviolet light, which the company analogizes to cement and water. Loading the player… This technology matters because future spacecraft will need to be larger in order to generate more electrical power and radiate a more heat into the vacuum of space, particularly if they’re going to serve as orbital data centers. But they’ll still need to fit into the tight confines of the fairing on top of the rocket that carries them into orbit. If spacecraft are able to construct their own structures in orbit, the power and heat-dissipation challenges may get a lot easier to solve. “Replicator 2 is the first proof that we can simply build the array in space, at whatever size the mission demands,” said Jakub Stojek, CEO and co-founder of Orbital Matter. The company is partnering with the European Space Agency and Thales Alenia, a leading European satellite builder, with which it collaborated on Replicator 2. Today’s large structures in space are origami projects — large solar arrays or telescope mirrors are folded up and then deployed on orbit. That’s a tricky engineering project, and so the idea of making and assembling those structures in space is appealing. NASA has funded some efforts at the idea, notably a mission with the company Redwire that 3D-printed structural beams in a vacuum chamber in 2023 but never got off the ground.
